content:
As part of the Special Campaign 6.0, the Agharkar Research Institute (ARI), Pune, is promoting scientific organic waste management, nutrient recycling and sustainable maintenance of green spaces across its campus. The Institute produces approximately 6,000 kg of compost annually from fallen leaves and garden waste and utilises it in its gardens. This initiative converts organic waste into a valuable soil amendment, promotes resource conservation and demonstrates the practical application of circular economy principles by returning organic matter and nutrients to the soil.
Fig 1:
Fallen leaves and palm fronds decomposing on the ARI campus, returning organic matter to the soil.
At ARI, fallen leaves and other garden residues are collected, crushed into smaller pieces and placed in a designated compost pit for in-house composting. The material is mixed weekly to facilitate aeration and microbial decomposition. Mature compost is harvested after approximately three to four months and used in the Institute’s gardens. During composting, microorganisms break down complex organic materials into more stable organic matter.
Fig 2:
Compost pits at ARI, Pune, where fallen leaves and garden residues are composted in-house.
At ARI, a mixture comprising 80% compost and 20% soil is used for gardening helping improve soil structure, enhancing water-holding capacity, contributing to soil organic matter and supporting nutrient availability for plants. The annual production and on-site utilisation of compost facilitate the productive reuse of locally available organic resources and help reduce the need for externally purchased gardening inputs. It also reduces the volume of garden waste requiring disposal and supports more resource-efficient campus management. On-site composting may further reduce waste transportation and the environmental impacts associated with landfill disposal.
ARI maintains approximately two acres of gardens and green areas, contributing to plant diversity, biodiversity conservation and the environmental quality of the campus. The Garden Section maintains approximately 308 trees representing more than 100 species, 39 medicinal plant species, 2,300 ornamental plants and 800 seasonal flowering plants, along with a variety of vegetables. The Institute’s Orchidarium supports the conservation and display of orchid diversity and facilitates specialised plant conservation and educational activities. The maintenance of diverse trees, medicinal plants and ornamental vegetation strengthens the campus’s green infrastructure and promotes awareness of plant diversity and conservation.
Complementing its waste management initiatives, ARI promotes nutrition-sensitive horticulture through its 6×6 Nutrition Garden Model. Designed for a compact area of 6 × 6 metres, the model demonstrates the cultivation of 23 types of vegetables through systematic crop planning and efficient utilisation of available space. Developed with the nutritional needs of a family of five to six members in mind, the model illustrates the potential of home gardening to improve access to fresh vegetables and promote dietary diversity and household nutrition security. The planned cultivation of diverse vegetables can support more varied diets and reduce dependence on externally sourced produce, subject to seasonal conditions and actual yields. The model offers potential for replication in urban, peri-urban and rural communities, particularly where land availability is limited. It integrates scientific crop planning, sustainable horticulture and household nutrition within a compact growing area.
Fig 3
: Nutrition Garden Model demonstrating scientific crop planning and efficient utilisation of garden space.
ARI’s initiatives demonstrate how scientific approaches to organic waste management, soil improvement, biodiversity conservation and nutrition-oriented gardening can contribute to a cleaner and greener institutional campus. By converting garden residues into compost and reusing the resulting material on-site, the Institute promotes waste minimisation, nutrient recycling and responsible resource management. These efforts reinforce the objectives of Special Campaign 6.0 by extending the concept of cleanliness beyond waste removal to include the scientific management and productive reuse of resources. ARI’s initiatives highlight the role of scientific institutions in translating environmental sustainability principles into practical campus-level action.

title: Unveiling the impact of black hole spin on flickering of light emitted from matter around the black hole
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 OCT 2026 4:54PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Scientists have uncovered a pivotal mechanism explaining why the matter around rapidly spinning black holes, also called accretion disk may emit highly oscillating X-rays.
The study which zeroes in on a single physical mechanism to produce these flickering of X-rays across a broad range of frequencies reduces randomness in theoretical modeling of these exotic astronomical objects.
Black hole, the most compact object in the Universe, with massive gravity that prevents even light from escaping, can spin about its axis. Matter pulled toward a black hole by its strong gravity is called an accretion flow and it falls inward at high speed, producing non-thermal radiation.
This radiation often shows nearly regular variations in brightness, called QPOs. In black hole X-ray binaries, these oscillations can have frequencies ranging from less than one cycle per second to several hundred cycles per second.
Previous studies could either explain the low frequency oscillations, or had to invoke other exotic process to explain high frequency oscillations.
In order to fill the gap, Scientists from the Aryabhatta Research Institute of Observational Sciences (ARIES), an autonomous institute of Department of Science and Technology (DST), Government of India took up the task of explaining how the oscillations of accretion shocks around a spinning black hole produce this wide range of frequencies.
They used a computer simulation developed by the Numerical and Theoretical Astrophysics Group at ARIES to model the behaviour of viscous accretion flows around black holes. Scientists from Nicolaus Copernicus Astronomical Center, Poland and MJP Rohilkhand University, Bareily were also involved in this work led by Mr. Sanit Debnath and Dr. Indranil Chattopadhyay from ARIES.
The simulation follows the movement of matter while ensuring that important physical quantities such as energy, mass, and momentum are conserved. This helped the researchers understand how these rapidly moving flows behave and how their oscillations can produce the observed variations in radiation from black holes.
Fig
:Time series of luminosity for two different
𝛼
=0.01, 0.035, and their corresponding power density spectrum (PDS) is shown for the model A91.2. We assume black hole mass is 10M
⊙
.
Their findings were recently published in the Journal of High Energy Astrophysics (JHEAP). The researchers found that when the viscosity of the accretion flow becomes higher than a certain critical value, the normally stable shock in the disc becomes unstable and starts to oscillate. These oscillations in the accretion disc can produce the regular variations in emitted radiation, observed as nearly periodic flickering of light know as quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs).
The study also revealed that the spin of a black hole has a strong influence on the movement of the shock and the frequency of QPOs. In slowly spinning black holes, viscosity pushes the average position of the oscillating shock farther away from the black hole, resulting mainly in low-frequency QPOs.
In contrast, rapidly spinning black holes pull the shock closer to the black hole, producing QPOs over a much wider range of frequencies. For black holes with very high spin the predicted QPO frequencies can exceed 100 Hz for a black hole about ten times the mass of the Sun, similar to the high-frequency variations observed in black hole X-ray binary systems.
The simulations also show that as the black hole spins faster, the shock moves closer to the black hole and its oscillations become more pronounced. Interestingly, the study found a clear relationship between the QPO frequency and the gradient of photon flux with the frequency or in other words the photons index, providing another useful clue for understanding the energetic environment around spinning black holes.
These findings provide a clear physical explanation for why rapidly spinning black holes in X-ray binary systems can produce high-frequency QPOs. According to the researchers, this is the first numerical study to simulate an accretion flow in presence of internal friction or viscosity and where the thermodynamic relations of a relativistic fluid has been implemented. This simulation demonstrates how the black hole’s spin can influence the frequency of QPOs, in the most realistic scenario.
The results can help scientists better understand the origin of the rapid variations in X-ray emission observed from these systems.

Sarbananda Sonowal
said.
The Maritime Development Fund (MDF), which has two components, is also taking shape. For its MIF component, SBI Ventures Limited has been appointed official Fund Manager. Registration as an Alternative Investment Fund with SEBI is due to be completed by the end of November, and the first close of Rs 5,000 crore is targeted by January, 2027.
The Interest Incentivisation Fund (IIF) is already delivering. Its online portal, www.iifmdf.in, is live, and loans of Rs 4,500 crore have been supported so far. About Rs 25 crore of interest subvention has been released against interest paid by borrowers.

’s
transformative Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047, India is building a stronger, more self-reliant and globally competitive maritime sector,"
Sonowal
said.

The Interest Incentivisation Fund eases the cost of borrowing for eligible shipyards, with SMFCL working out the incentive, running the application and claims portal, and releasing the interest support. Under the Shipbuilding Development Scheme, the credit risk cover corpus is managed centrally and backed by premium and claims review, giving shipyards and lenders a safety net against payment risk.
SMFCL's own lending appraises, sanctions and monitors projects across ports, rail and road links, inland waterways, coastal infrastructure, port-hinterland logistics, shipbuilding and ship repair. title: From Critical Overdose To Sustained Recovery
subtitle: Kamrup Assam’s Amit’s Journey Of Hope And Rehabilitation
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 OCT 2026 7:12PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Timely medical intervention, evidence-based treatment and continued family support plays an important role in helping individuals overcome substance dependence and rebuild their lives.
The journey of Amit
(Name Changed),
a 31-year-old man from Kamrup Metropolitan district of Assam, highlights how coordinated medical care and sustained rehabilitation can support long-term recovery and social reintegration.
Amit is a graduate and self-employed individual whose journey towards recovery began following a life-threatening heroin overdose. He was admitted to the emergency department of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Guwahati, with severe respiratory depression requiring urgent medical attention. During his hospitalisation, he was also diagnosed with Hepatitis C. His opioid dependence had significantly affected his health and overall well-being, making timely and comprehensive treatment essential.
Despite these challenges, Amit remained motivated to overcome substance dependence. The encouragement and practical support of his family played an important role in helping him continue treatment and work towards recovery. Following initial stabilisation, he was shifted to the Neuropsychiatry ward, where he was initiated on Opioid Substitution Therapy (OST) using buprenorphine. He also received medical care for Hepatitis C and underwent relapse prevention therapy, addressing both his medical needs and the psychosocial challenges associated with substance dependence.
After discharge, Amit continued treatment under medical supervision, including buprenorphine-naloxone medication, psychosocial interventions, nursing support and regular follow-up consultations. Continuous monitoring and counselling helped him adhere to his treatment plan and maintain progress towards recovery. The coordinated approach ensured that his treatment extended beyond emergency care to include ongoing support for his physical and psychological well-being.
An important milestone in Amit’s rehabilitation was securing employment within two to three months of recovery. This achievement enabled him to resume productive activities, contribute financially to his family and regain greater stability in his personal and social life. His progress demonstrated how appropriate treatment and continued support can help individuals rebuild their livelihoods and move towards greater independence.
Amit has maintained adherence to treatment and abstinence from substance use for over a year without relapse. With his recovery progressing steadily, his medication doses are now being gradually reduced under medical supervision. His journey reflects the importance of timely emergency care, evidence-based treatment, relapse prevention, regular follow-up and family involvement in supporting sustained recovery from substance dependence.
Through the Addiction Treatment Facility (ATF) at AIIMS Guwahati, Amit received coordinated medical and psychosocial support that helped him move from a life-threatening emergency towards sustained recovery. His experience highlights the importance of accessible treatment and rehabilitation services in helping individuals regain their health, strengthen family relationships, rebuild livelihoods and reintegrate into society. His journey offers a message of hope that, with appropriate treatment, continued support and personal commitment, recovery from substance dependence is possible.

The Mela is
showcasing India’s rich and diverse heritage of traditional handicrafts and handloom products.
Organized by the Ministry of
Social Justice and Empowerment, Government of India, the Mela will continue until October 28 Wednesday.
A Senior Official in the Ministry said the Mela remains open to public at Farm Gate, Khanapara, Guwahati, from 11 A.M. onwards till 9 O’ Clock. He said the visitors are exploring the diverse range of traditional products to purchase the creations and support the artisans.
The visitors are also enthralled to witness a galaxy of artists presenting traditional musical and dance programmes.

He said the event is providing participating artisans with a platform to exhibit and sell their products directly to visitors, establish connections with prospective customers and explore opportunities to expand their market reach.
By facilitating direct interaction between artisans and consumers, the Mela seeks to strengthen market access, encourage entrepreneurship and improve livelihood opportunities for participating artisans, he added.
The Official said the Guwahati edition features a wide range of traditional crafts and handloom products representing different regions of India.
The participation of artisans from the North-Eastern States, alongside those from other parts of the country, will provide visitors with an opportunity to appreciate the diversity of India’s artistic traditions, indigenous craftsmanship and cultural heritage, he added.
He said the event aims to also encourage greater appreciation of the skills and creativity of artisans whose work contributes to preserving traditional knowledge and craft practices.

BHARAT-TULIP (Traditional Artisans’ Upliftment Livelihood Programme)

It also supports the preservation and promotion of traditional arts and crafts by connecting artisans and their products with evolving consumer markets, he said.
The Shilp Samagam Mela (SSM-2026) is an important initiative of the Ministry to provide marketing support to artisans and beneficiaries associated with its three National Corporations: the National Scheduled Castes Finance and Development Corporation (NSFDC), the National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC), and the National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation (NBCFDC).

Guided by the vision of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s principle of

content:
Under the Integrated Programme for Senior Citizens (IPSrC) of Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY) implemented by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, the financial assistance is provided through a grant-in-aid mechanism to eligible organizations, including Non-Governmental Organizations, State Governments, Panchayati Raj Institutions and local bodies. The same is aimed for establishing and maintaining facilities for senior citizens. At present, 764 Senior Citizen Homes, 13 Continuous Care Homes, 17 Mobile Medicare Units and 3 Physiotherapy Clinics are being supported under IPSrC.
These facilities provide residential care and support services, with particular emphasis on ensuring shelter and care for indigent senior citizens. The programme also supports mobile healthcare services, physiotherapy facilities and other interventions aimed at improving the well-being of elderly persons. Financial assistance is released to eligible implementing organizations in accordance with the scheme’s provisions.
An Official in the Ministry said the Integrated Programme for Senior Citizens (IPSrC) is one of the key components besides the State Action Plan for Senior Citizens (SAPSrC) and Regional Resource and Training Centres (RRTCs) under the  Yojana, which collectively supports the delivery of services and strengthen institutions involved in senior citizen welfare.
He said the Yojana is aimed to promote the welfare of senior citizens through an integrated framework of care services, institutional support and state-level initiatives. The scheme addresses the diverse needs of elderly persons, particularly indigent senior citizens, by supporting residential care facilities, strengthening geriatric care capacities and promoting awareness and evidence-based interventions on ageing-related issues.
The Official said the Regional Resource and Training Centres (RRTCs) serve as important institutional support structures under AVYAY, particularly in facilitating the implementation of IPSrC.
He added that as provided under the scheme guidelines, annual financial support of ₹19.58 lakh is extended to each RRTC. The Ministry also provides financial assistance to designated NGOs and institutions functioning as RRTCs to strengthen outreach, capacity building and service delivery for senior citizens.
Designated by the Government, these centres function as regional nodal agencies for capacity building, training, research, documentation, awareness generation and advocacy on ageing and senior citizen welfare, the Official further said.
RRTCs support evidence-based planning and programme implementation through database development, monitoring and evaluation, project inspections, and coordination with State Governments, Union Territories and implementing organisations.
Under AVYAY, the State Action Plan for Senior Citizens focuses on strengthening state-level planning, implementation and capacity building for elderly welfare. Under this component, financial assistance is provided to State and Union Territory Governments for initiatives such as developing a pool of trained geriatric caregivers, organising special cataract surgery drives and implementing other approved welfare interventions suited to local requirements.
To encourage local innovation and address state-specific needs, States and Union Territories may utilise up to 20 per cent of their allocated funds for state-specific programmes, subject to the scheme’s provisions. Funding is admissible only for components approved under AVYAY. States and Union Territories are also expected to contribute their own resources to supplement the funds available for these initiatives.
Through its integrated components, AVYAY combines institutional care, state-level planning and regional capacity building to address the varied needs of India’s ageing population. The scheme supports the development and maintenance of care facilities, encourages locally responsive welfare interventions and strengthens the institutions involved in implementing programmes for senior citizens, with an emphasis on dignity, care and improved access to welfare services.

title: Changes in PLFS schedule and estimation procedure from January 2027 - inviting comments thereon
subtitle: NSO to introduce changes in PLFS from January 2027
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 OCT 2026 12:14PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Statistics Office (NSO), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), has been conducting the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) since 2017. PLFS has evolved to meet the demand for more timely and disaggregated labour market statistics. The sampling design of PLFS was revamped from January 2025 to provide monthly, quarterly and annual estimates and to enable estimation of indicators at sub-state level. Education and skilling questions were added, and also information on digital platform workers, a subset of gig workers, has been collected on an experimental basis since January 2026.
The NSO proposes to introduce modification in the sampling design of the PLFS from January 2027, when fresh samples for the two-year period 2027-2028 (new Panel 6) will be drawn from an updated sampling frame. It also introduces certain changes in the survey schedule. A concept note giving the details has been prepared and is available at
https://www.mospi.gov.in/
.
Comments and suggestions are invited from the policymakers, researchers, academic and research institutions and members of the general public on the proposed modifications within 15 days from the date of publication of this press note.
Key changes in sampling design and estimation
Separate stratum for digital platform workers.
Experience from PLFS 2026 showed that the existing arrangement did not capture an adequate number of digital platform workers. A new Second Stage Stratum (SSS) based on digital platform work is being introduced, while the existing SSS structure and composition are retained. There will be four SSSs in rural areas and five in urban areas, with 14 households canvassed in each selected First Stage Unit (FSU). This revision in SSS formation is expected to improve the coverage of digital platform workers and facilitate more comprehensive data collection on this emerging segment of the labour market.
Updated sampling frame and refinements.
Fresh samples for the two-year period 2027-2028 (Panel 6) will be drawn from an updated frame reflecting the updated Urban Frame Survey, urbanisation and de-urbanisation, and the creation, splitting or merger of districts and other administrative units, along with follow-up updation of the rural Census 2011 frame. The updated sampling frame will ensure better representation of the current population, urban population in particular, by capturing changes in urbanisation, administrative boundaries and the emergence of new urban areas. It is expected to improve sample coverage and enhance the reliability and relevance of PLFS estimates.
Additionally, criteria for sample allocation and stratification have also been modified/ updated based on the experience of the previous two-year period (Panel 5). These revisions are expected to improve the efficiency of sample allocation and stratification and ensure better representation of population variations which in turn minimise operational difficulties during sample selection.
Transition in the first three months.
For the first three months from January 2027, the sample will comprise FSUs from both the Panel 5 frame and the updated Panel 6 frame. Pooled monthly estimates based on both frames will be presented in the monthly bulletins for these months. Relative Standard Error (RSE) estimates will not be presented for these three months. This approach will facilitate a smooth transition to the updated sampling frame while ensuring continuity in the release of monthly and quarterly labour market estimates.
Key changes in the PLFS schedule
Identifying digital platform workers.
An additional binary question has been introduced in Block 5 of Schedule 0.0PL, to identify households in which any member has ever engaged in digital platform work during the specified reference period. The questions will be canvassed in all urban as well as rural households to facilitate the identification of eligible households for formation of the new digital platform workers based SSS.
Measuring unpaid activities.
New questions have been added to Schedule 10.4 on own-use production of goods, unpaid household and caregiving activities, volunteer work and unpaid trainee work. These items will be canvassed in both rural and urban areas during the first visit only, for persons aged 15 years and above, thereby enabling annual reporting on these activities. The inclusion of these items will facilitate a more comprehensive assessment of different forms of work beyond conventional employment, improve the availability of data on unpaid and non-market activities and support a broader understanding of the contribution of individuals to household and community well-being.
The modified sampling design and estimation procedure and the modified Schedules 0.0PL and 10.4 form part of the concept note.

MOIL recorded its highest-ever H1 manganese ore production of 0.96 Mt in April–September 2026, surpassing its previous H1 record of 0.943 Mt. The milestone strengthens the domestic availability of manganese ore, a key raw material for the steel industry.

7. International Co-operation
Ministry of Steel officials and representatives from NMDC, SAIL, MOIL and MECON participated in the India Pavilion at Russian Energy Week 2026 in Moscow from 14 to 16 October, where India was the partner country. The delegation held discussions with officials of the Russian Ministry of Energy on bilateral cooperation, coal security and strategic investment opportunities, and participated in an India–Russia Energy Dialogue roundtable.
On the sidelines, NMDC explored cooperation with Russian companies in critical minerals and mining technologies, and invited Russian equipment manufacturers to establish manufacturing facilities in India. MOIL held discussions with Russian technology companies on AI-driven digitalisation of mining operations, while MECON signed an MoU with Zyfra LLC for digitalisation and automation solutions in the mining, metals and energy sectors. MECON also explored cooperation on steel mill rolls and on sintering and pelletisation technologies for projects in India.
8. Green Steel Initiatives
Under the Ministry of Steel’s Green Steel Initiative, 104 distinct steel producers have been issued Green Steel Certificates across the lists issued up to October 2026. The certification covers products including TMT bars, HR/CR coils, plates, wire rods, pipes and other steel products, with a large majority of certified products receiving 5-star ratings, reflecting the growing adoption of lower-emission steelmaking practices across India’s steel industry.
NMDC signed a Gas Sales Agreement with GAIL Gas Limited for the supply of re-gasified liquefied natural gas (RLNG) to its pellet plant at Nagarnar, Jagdalpur. The switch from furnace oil is expected to ensure clean and reliable energy supply, reduce emissions and improve operational efficiency.

title: Third Regional Review Conference on Forest Rights Act Implementation Held in Srinagar
subtitle: Seven States/UT review pending claims, recognition of forest rights, Community Forest Resource Rights and livelihood convergence; time-bound action plans emphasised
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 OCT 2026 8:43PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MoTA), Government of India, convened the Third Regional Review Conference on the implementation of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA), in Srinagar, Jammu & Kashmir, today. Senior officials from Maharashtra, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Goa, Rajasthan and Jammu & Kashmir reviewed implementation progress, discussed challenges and identified priority actions. The conference concluded the regional review series, following the first conference in Bengaluru on 10 September 2026 and the second in Kolkata on 9 October 2026.
Shri Mohd Mumtaz Ali, Director, Tribal Affairs Department, Government of Jammu & Kashmir, delivered the welcome address, highlighting the region’s difficult terrain, dispersed settlements and seasonal pastoral movements, and the need for locally appropriate administrative arrangements.
Shri Javed Ahmed Rana, Hon’ble Minister for Tribal Affairs, Jal Shakti and Forest, Ecology & Environment, Government of Jammu & Kashmir, emphasised that the FRA safeguards the dignity, livelihoods and future of forest-dependent communities. He called for transparent and timely claim disposal, stronger interdepartmental coordination and greater Gram Sabha participation, stressing that forest rights recognition, conservation and sustainable development must advance together.
In the keynote address, Shri Anant Prakash Pandey, Joint Secretary, MoTA, reported that, as of 31 August 2026, approximately 54 lakh claims had been received nationally, 43.56 lakh (80.64%) disposed of, 25.42 lakh titles distributed over nearly 238 lakh acres, 10.45 lakh claims pending and 18.13 lakh rejected. He stressed that every rejection must be supported by a reasoned order communicated to the claimant, with statutory appeal rights preserved, and urged States to prepare district-wise plans to expedite pending claims and review rejected cases, particularly in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa and Himachal Pradesh.
Highlighting Community Forest Resource Rights (CFRR), he called for sustainable management and convergence of CFR Management Plans with Forest Department Working Plans, enabled by the joint communication of MoTA and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change dated 27 July 2026. Incorporating recognised rights into revenue records can facilitate access to PM-KISAN and agriculture, fisheries and livelihood schemes. He also urged States to expedite Habitat Rights recognition for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), noting that rights have so far been recognised for only 11 of the country’s 75 PVTGs. Other priorities included quarterly State Level Monitoring Committee (SLMC) meetings, regular Monthly Progress Reports, integration of State FRA records with the National FRA Portal through Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), and use of free FRA courses on iGOT for awareness and capacity building.
Smt. Samidha Singh, Director (FRA), MoTA, outlined financial assistance of ₹25 lakh per State under the Support to Tribal Research Institutes scheme for FRA mapping and ₹15 lakh per Community Forest Resource Management Plan under DA-JGUA, along with ₹1 lakh for technical support. She also highlighted support for PVTG Habitat Rights under Ministry guidelines dated 5 January 2026, urging States to reconcile data discrepancies, strengthen Gram Sabhas, raise awareness, provide post-claim support and facilitate CFR Management Plans.
State-wise progress
Maharashtra:
The State has distributed 2,03,510 individual and 8,821 community titles against 3,90,397 individual and 10,740 community claims; CFR rights cover approximately 13.87 lakh acres, with 7,518 CFR Committees constituted and 1,875 management plans prepared. A Government Resolution dated 10 July 2026 provides separate Village Forms 7-E and 12-E for Individual Forest Rights (IFR) holders, facilitating crop loans, Kisan Credit Cards, crop insurance and Direct Benefit Transfer; success stories from Jalgaon, Thane and Nashik highlighted improvements in farm income and water security.
Gadchiroli, Maharashtra:
The district has distributed 34,813 titles (33,361 individual and 1,452 CFR) covering over 5.56 lakh hectares, including 5.16 lakh hectares under CFR rights; 1,442 CFR Committees have been constituted for 1,138 CFR Gram Sabhas, and 391 management plans approved. It has entered 32,601 IFR titles in 7/12 revenue records, scanned 99.6% of case files and trained 3,630 Gram Sabha representatives through Project Ekal with Gondwana University; mapping by ISB Hyderabad estimated annual non-timber forest produce potential at ₹98 crore. Proposals included a dedicated CFR budget, committee guidelines, an online NTFP sales platform and alignment of Working Plans with CFR Management Plans.
Gujarat:
The State has distributed 1,00,747 individual and 3,879 community titles against 1,83,055 individual and 6,274 community claims, with CFR rights covering approximately 10.18 lakh acres. Satellite verification with the GEER Foundation and State-sponsored FRA Cells is addressing pendency in Dahod, Sabarkantha, Panchmahal, Mahisagar and Chhota Udepur. Identified PVTGs include Kotwalia, Kolgha, Kathodi, Siddi and Padhar; the State will submit a Habitat Rights Action Plan to MoTA.
Jammu & Kashmir:
Of 48,287 claims received, 6,191 have been approved by District Level Committees (DLCs) and 6,178 titles distributed, covering approximately 3,960 hectares, predominantly under community rights. The UT has an SLMC under the Chief Secretary, DLCs in all 20 districts and a circular dated 30 July 2026 directing that eligible ST and OTFD families not be evicted before due process is completed. It sought clarifications on the continuation of non-official SDLC/DLC members after District Development Council terms expire, Gram Sabha quorum, satellite imagery as evidence, a one-time window to review rejected claims, and funds for awareness and capacity building.
Himachal Pradesh:
Up to March 2026, the State had granted 1,144 individual and 166 community titles against 6,546 individual and 791 community claims, with community rights covering 27,624 hectares, mainly in Chamba and Kinnaur. Record-entry instructions were issued in April 2022 for community titles and February 2026 for individual titles; the State launched an FRA Calendar in April 2025, conducted workshops and held three SLMC meetings. DLC and SDLC meetings at least three times a month are planned following committee reconstitution after the May 2026 Panchayat elections.
Uttar Pradesh:
The State has distributed 22,537 individual and 893 community titles against 92,972 individual and 1,194 community claims, with 14,339 titles incorporated into records. It is reviewing rejected claims, particularly in Sonbhadra and Chandauli, has set 30 January 2027 as the deadline for completing record incorporation in the remaining districts, and identified the Buxa PVTG in Bijnor.
Goa:
The State has distributed 3,908 individual and 29 community titles against 9,983 individual and 401 community claims. It launched its FRA Atlas on 25 May 2026, engaged a private agency for surveys and demarcation, constituted special committees under Joint Mamlatdars in six talukas and provided spot-verification allowances to Forest Rights Committee (FRC) members. Revenue records are updated suo motu after title distribution, with DLCs meeting fortnightly and SDLCs weekly.
Rajasthan:
As of 30 September 2026, the State had distributed 49,383 individual and 2,531 community titles against 1,21,707 individual and 5,433 community claims. Of these, 40,045 titles have been incorporated into revenue and forest records, while 11,869 incorporations remain pending.
Way forward
MoTA called upon States and the UT to prepare district-wise action plans identifying the stage and cause of delay and the responsible authority for each pending claim; review rejected claims with written reasons and the right of petition; submit reconciled Monthly Progress Reports regularly; and complete digitisation and incorporation of recognised rights into revenue and forest records in accordance with the advisory dated 24 June 2026. They were also asked to develop PVTG-wise Habitat Rights roadmaps, strengthen convergence with livelihood and welfare schemes, prepare capacity-building action plans and review progress quarterly through SLMCs chaired by the Chief Secretary.
The conference concluded with a valedictory address by the Joint Secretary, MoTA, followed by a vote of thanks by the Deputy Director, Tribal Research Institute, Jammu & Kashmir UT Administration.

title: Agri-Voltaics
subtitle: Powering India’s Farms, Growing a Sustainable Future
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 OCT 2026 11:24AM by PIB Delhi
content:
At the intersection of agriculture and renewable energy lies an innovative approach to making farmland more productive. Agrivoltaics combines crop cultivation with solar power generation on the same land, enabling farmers to diversify their incomes while contributing to India’s clean energy transition. By bringing food production and solar electricity together, it offers a promising pathway towards efficient land use, greater farm resilience and sustainable rural prosperity.
Solar Power for Agri Farms and a Cleaner Future
Agriculture plays a vital role in India’s economy, serving as a key source of livelihood for approximately 46.1 per cent of the population.
The Gross Value Added (GVA) of the Agriculture and Allied Sector is estimated to reach
Rs. 52.08 lakh crore in 2025-26
. Sustaining this vital sector requires reliable and affordable energy for irrigation and other farming operations. Solar power can help meet these everyday needs while advancing India’s clean energy transition.
Click to Read More: The New Era of Indian Agriculture and Allied Sectors
India’s vast agricultural land offers significant prospects to integrate solar energy with farming. According to
Land Use Statistics for 2023-24
, the country’s reported area covers
306.96 million hectares
, of which approximately
55 per cent is agricultural land
. The
net sown area stands at 138.99 million hectares
, while the
gross cropped area covers 217.88 million hectares
. This extensive land base offers opportunities to generate solar electricity alongside agricultural production. Farmers can use solar power to operate
irrigation pumps, reduce dependence on conventional electricity and potentially supplementary revenue
by supplying surplus electricity to the grid. For instance, solar-powered irrigation pumps can provide daytime power for watering crops while reducing reliance on diesel-powered alternatives.
Agrivoltaics takes this integration further by bringing together crop cultivation and solar electricity generation on the same land.
Solar panels installed above or between crop rows allow electricity generation alongside continued farming. Depending on the crop, panel design and local conditions, partial shading may also help reduce soil moisture loss. This approach can improve land-use efficiency, diversify farm earnings and strengthening both food and energy security. Through research, field demonstrations and policy development, India is exploring ways to adapt agrivoltaics to diverse agricultural conditions. It offers a promising pathway to align farmers’ livelihoods with India’s wider renewable energy ambitions
.
The
7th AGRIVOLTAICS WORLD CONFERENCE
, being held In New Delhi on 21–23 October 2026 under the theme
“Powering the Global South,”
serves as a global platform to advance the integration of solar energy and agriculture. Convening stakeholders from industry, research, policy and finance, the conference focuses on emerging opportunities in agrivoltaics to promote efficient land use, strengthen agricultural sustainability and support the transition towards a low-carbon economy.
Read more about
7th AgriVoltaics World Conference
Agrivoltaics: Bridging Agriculture and Renewable Energy
Agrivoltaics, also known as
agrisolar
or
dual-use solar
, maximises land-use efficiency, provides shade for crops and creates additional benefits for farmers.
Design and Functioning of Agrivoltaic Systems
An agrivoltaic system integrates agricultural infrastructure with solar installations, adapted to local farming conditions. The technology operates through various key elements:
Elevated Solar Structures:
Instead of placing solar panels directly on the ground, they are mounted on structures high enough to let sunlight and rain reach the crops below. These elevated solar panels for agriculture also allow farmers to move their equipment underneath without any trouble.
Partial shading:
The panels provide shade, which helps protect crops from extreme heat and reduces water evaporation from the soil. This creates a cooler, more stable environment for plants to grow, especially in hot or dry regions.
Dual Land Productivity:
Agrivoltaics optimises land use by integrating crop cultivation or livestock rearing with solar power generation, supplying electricity for farm activities and creating an additional revenue stream through surplus power sales to the grid.
Agrivoltaics Development in India
As of August 2025, India had
36 operational agrivoltaics projects
with an
installed capacity of 37.54 megawatts, alongside 10 pilot projects under development
. These Projects span diverse agroclimatic regions and include elevated structures, interspace layouts and tracking systems, reflecting India’s evolving approach to integrating solar power generation with agricultural production.
India’s Agrivoltaic Potential
India holds significant potential for agrivoltaics.
Estimates place the country’s agrivoltaic potential between
3,000 GW and nearly 14,000 GW
, highlighting the scale of opportunity at the intersection of agriculture and renewable energy. Agrivoltaic systems can also create profits diversification for farmers. In some cases, annual earnings could rise from around
₹
60,000 per acre to over
₹
1 lakh per acre
.
Scope for Agrivoltaics Developments
Land Suitability:
The GIS-based national screening identified
47.35 million hectares
of “restricted cropland” suitable for AgriPV after applying environmental, agronomic, and technical filters, reflecting a conservative, climate-resilient land base.
Crop Compatibility:
Fruits, vegetables, spices and medicinal plants offer promising options for cultivation alongside solar installations.
High-potential states
include Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh, which collectively account for nearly 50 per cent of India’s estimated AgriPV power generation potential, driven
by favourable combination of cropland availability, solar resource, and agro-climatic conditions.
Moderate potential
is observed in Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Telangana, Bihar, and West Bengal.
The southern, western, and central regions exhibit the most favourable combination of solar irradiance, land availability, and horticultural intensity for large-scale deployment.
Government Initiatives in Agrivoltaics Development
The Government of India has undertaken a range of policy, research, technology development, and implementation measures to advance agrivoltaics adoption and expansion across the country.
Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (PM KUSUM):
Launched in February 2019, the scheme encourages solar energy adoption in agriculture, reduces dependence on diesel and creates opportunities for farmers to diversify their earnings. It envisages central financial assistance of approximately ₹34,422 crore. It also enables decentralised solar power generation and solarisation of agricultural pumps, creating avenues of development for solar energy integration with farming.
PM KUSUM Scheme
Centre of Excellence on Agrivoltaics:
The National Institute of Solar Energy, in collaboration with the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s Indian Agricultural Research Institute, has established a CoE for agrivoltaics research, demonstration and capacity building. It has undertaken pilot projects, including a 100-kilowatt agrivoltaic system at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute.
India Agrivoltaics Alliance
The
India Agrivoltaics Alliance (IAA
), anchored by the National Solar Energy Federation of India (NSEFI), is a multi-stakeholder platform advancing the dual use of land for solar energy generation and agriculture. Launched in 2023, the Alliance has grown to over 40 members and works with government ministries and industry stakeholders to advance agrivoltaics through policy advocacy, research and on-the-ground implementation. It develops knowledge resources, promotes pilot projects and supports scalable business models to improve land productivity, diversify farmer incomes and strengthen rural energy access.
State-specific Initiatives
Several states are facilitating solar energy in agriculture through region-specific schemes.
Mukhyamantri Saur Krushi Vahini Yojana 2.0, Maharashtra:
The scheme drives solar power generation through 16,000 megawatts of solar projects across approximately 35,000 acres of government and private land to support electricity supply to agricultural consumers.
Kisan Suryoday Yojana, Gujarat:
Expands solar energy utilisation to meet farmers’ electricity needs by providing daytime power supply for agricultural activities, with a planned supply window of up to 16 hours daily, from 5:00 AM to 9:00 PM, through the phased commissioning of solar and other non-conventional energy generation plants.
Surya Raitha Scheme, Karnataka
:
The scheme advances solar-powered irrigation pumps and allows farmers to earn from surplus electricity. Solar pumps can help farmers access energy for watering their crops while reducing dependence on diesel-powered pumps.
The Government of India, alongside state governments, is advancing the use of solar energy in agriculture through policy measures and targeted programmes. These efforts are shaping India’s agrivoltaics landscape by creating opportunities for the co-location of solar power generation and agricultural production.
Powering Prosperity Through the Convergence of Farms and Clean Energy
Agrivoltaics offers India an opportunity to strengthen agricultural livelihoods while advancing environmental sustainability. By combining food production with renewable energy generation, it can offer scope for more efficient land use, conserve water under suitable conditions and create greater financial resilience. The Government of India’s initiatives, including PM-KUSUM and proposed measures to expand agrivoltaics, reflect efforts to connect rural development with clean energy goals. As implementation grows, locally suitable designs, scientific research and farmer participation will be essential to balance agricultural productivity with energy needs. This approach can contribute to a more resilient and sustainable future for India. Greater financial resilience

title: Department of Pharmaceuticals Constitutes Committee to Review Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices
subtitle:
Committee to Examine UCPMP Framework and Recommend Measures for Strengthening Oversight Mechanisms;

To submit report within 2 months from the date of its first meeting
ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :Department of Pharmaceuticals
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 OCT 2026 6:42PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, has
constituted a Committee
to comprehensively examine the existing
regulatory framework governing pharmaceutical marketing practices
and recommend measures to
strengthen oversight, monitoring and enforcement mechanisms to curb unethical practices in the pharmaceutical sector
.
Dr. M. Srinivas, Member, NITI Aayog
has been named as the Chairperson of the committee with
Smt. Preeti Sudan, Former Union Health Secretary
, and
Dr. Naresh Trehan, CMD, Medanta
, as its members. The Committee will have to submit its recommendations within a period of two months from the date of its first meeting, after undertaking the requisite consultative process.
The
Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP)
was introduced in
2015
as a voluntary,
industry-led self-regulatory
mechanism to promote ethical pharmaceutical marketing and regulate interactions between pharmaceutical companies and healthcare professionals. The Department subsequently introduced UCPMP 2024, which superseded the 2015 version and strengthened the implementation framework. The 2024 Code is currently in operation.
The Committee will undertake a comprehensive examination of issues relating to unethical pharmaceutical marketing practices and make recommendations on the following
Terms of Reference (ToR)
:
a) To undertake a holistic and comprehensive examination of all issues relating to unethical pharmaceutical marketing practices.
b) To examine the efficacy of the existing mechanisms for monitoring, oversight and enforcement with respect to unethical pharma marketing practices, and to identify measures required to ensure greater transparency, accountability and effective compliance.
c) To examine the need for measures required to strengthen the existing monitoring and regulatory framework and to suggest appropriate regulatory/statutory or any other measures and legal framework for implementation of such measures as necessary.
d) To discuss with concerned stakeholders, technical, professional and domain experts, institutions or bodies, as considered necessary and consider their submissions objectively while submitting its recommendations on the matter after a comprehensive examination.
e) To deliberate and recommend on any other relevant issue in connection with curbing unethical pharma marketing practices.
